body:
Childhood & Early Life

John Wilmot was born on April 1, 1647, at Ditchley in Oxfordshire, in the middle of a civil war his father was on the losing side of. Henry Wilmot was a Royalist cavalry commander who later helped the young Charles II escape England after the battle of Worcester, and was made Earl of Rochester for it. He died in exile in 1658, so John became the second earl at ten, with a title, a mother who was devout and strict, and very little money. He started at Wadham College, Oxford, at twelve and was given his master's degree at fourteen. Then he went off to France and Italy, which finished the job of making him unmanageable.

What He Did & Why He's Remembered

Rochester was the most brilliant and the most dangerous wit at the court of Charles II. He wrote satires so sharp they got him banished more than once, love songs that are still tender, and a long string of obscene poems that kept some editors away for centuries. Under all the swagger he was a real philosopher of disappointment. He doubted reason, doubted love, doubted himself, and wrote about all three better than almost anyone of his time. He was a rake, a drunk, a soldier, a playwright's patron, and once, for a stretch, a fake doctor.

Family Life

He married, but only after a scandal. In 1665 he tried to abduct a rich young heiress, Elizabeth Malet, and was thrown in the Tower for it. They married in 1667 anyway. Elizabeth stayed with him through everything, raised their children (Anne, Charles, Elizabeth and Malet) mostly in the country while he stayed in London, and their surviving letters are affectionate and funny. He also had a daughter with the actress Elizabeth Barry, who he coached into being one of the great stage stars of her age.

Romantic Life

He loved his wife and betrayed her constantly, and seems to have known exactly how that looked. Elizabeth Barry was his protegee and lover. His poems keep circling one idea, that desire is real and lasting faithfulness is the thing nobody can promise. The first poem below shows the other side of him. It is a plain, almost frightened vow written by a man who knows his own habits.

Life Until Death

In the 1660s he fought at sea against the Dutch and was praised for his nerve. At the start of the 1670s he disguised himself as a mountebank called Doctor Bendo and sold potions near the Tower of London. He wrote a lampoon on the king himself, and some say he once handed Charles the wrong paper by mistake. Years of drinking and disease wore him down, and by thirty he was ill and looked much older. In his last months he talked with the clergyman Gilbert Burnet about God, nature and the soul, and in the end repented. He died on July 26, 1680, at Woodstock Park, aged 33. His poems appeared in print the same year.

His Works

Song (Absent from thee)

I
Absent from thee I languish still;
Then ask me not,
When I return?
The straying Fool 'twill plainly kill,
To wish all Day, all Night to mourn.

II
Dear; from thine Arms then let me flie,
That my fantastick Mind may prove The Torments it deserves to try,
That tears my fix'd Heart from my Love.

III
When weary'd with a World of Woe To thy safe Bosom I retire,
Where Love, and Peace, and Truth does flow,
May I contented there expire.

IV
Lest once more wand'ring from that Heav'n,
I fall on some base Heart unblest;
Faithless to thee, false, unforgiven,
And lose my everlasting Rest.

Upon Nothing

I
Nothing! thou Elder Brother ev'n to Shade,
That hadst a Being ere the World was made,
And (well fixt) art alone, of Ending not afraid.

II
Ere Time and Place were,
Time and Place were not,
When Primitive Nothing something streight begot,
Then all proceeded from the great united—What.

III
Something, the gen'ral Attribute of all,
Sever'd from thee, its sole Original,
Into thy boundless self must undistinguish'd fall.

IV
Yet Something did thy mighty Pow'r command,
And from thy fruitful Emptiness's Hand,
Snatch'd Men,
Beasts,
Birds,
Fire,
Air and Land.

V
Matter, the wickedst Off-spring of thy Race,
By Form assisted, flew from thy Embrace,
And Rebel Light obscur'd thy reverend dusky Face.

VI
With Form and Matter,
Time and Place did join;
Body, thy foe, with thee did Leagues combine,
To spoil thy peaceful Realm, and ruin all thy Line.

VII
But Turn-coat Time assists the Foe in vain,
And, brib'd by thee, assists thy short-liv'd Reign,
And to thy hungry Womb drives back thy Slaves again.

VIII
Tho' Mysteries are barr'd from Laick Eyes,
And the Divine alone, with Warrant, pries Into thy Bosom, where the Truth in private lies:

IX
Yet this of thee the Wise may freely say,
Thou from the Virtuous nothing tak'st away,
And to be part with thee the Wicked wisely pray.

X
Great Negative, how vainly would the Wise Enquire, define, distinguish, teach, devise?
Didst thou not stand to point their dull Philosophies.

XI
Is, or is not, the Two great Ends of Fate,
And, true or false, the Subject of Debate,
That perfect, or destroy, the vast Designs of Fate;

XII
When they have rack'd the Politician's Breast,
Within thy Bosom most securely rest,
And, when reduc'd to thee, are least unsafe and best.

XIII
But,
Nothing, why does Something still permit,
That Sacred Monarchs should at Council sit,
With Persons highly thought at best for nothing fit?

XIV
Whilst weighty Something modestly abstains,
From Princes Coffers, and from Statesmens Brains,
And Nothing there like stately Nothing reigns.

XV
Nothing, who dwell'st with Fools in grave Disguise,
For whom they reverend Shapes, and Forms devise,
Lawn Sleeves, and Furs, and Gowns, when they like thee look wise.

XVI
French Truth,
Dutch Prowess,
British Policy,
Hibernian Learning,
Scotch Civility,
Spaniards Dispatch,
Danes Wit, are mainly seen in thee.

XVII
The Great Man's Gratitude to his best Friend,
Kings Promises,
Whores Vows, towards thee they bend,
Flow swiftly into thee, and in thee ever end.

On Charles II (an epitaph, as attributed)

Here lies our sovereign lord the King,
Whose word no man relies on,
Who never said a foolish thing,
Nor ever did a wise one.
epi: The libertine who wrote the most honest love song and the most honest poem about nothing
quote: Nothing! thou Elder Brother ev'n to Shade, / That hadst a Being ere the World was made
